wi_11_vulture_lookout_east.blurb: A small bouldering zone on the south-facing side of the East Bluff above Devil's Lake, in the Baraboo Range. Eighteen problems are spread among trees and scattered blocks below a lookout bench, with a friendly bottom end of VB to V2 and a thinner top end that climbs into the V8 to V10 range. The bulk of what is here sits between V0 and V5, so it suits a mixed group. Tree cover keeps parts of it shaded, though some lines catch morning light. The walk in is a good stretch of trail, and the neighbouring Vulture Lookout West is only a minute or two further along.

wa_main_wall_13.blurb: The main face of the Cliff Drive crag, set on the basalt bluff right inside Spokane, with the city laid out below. Eighteen short, bolted routes make up the wall: mostly sport leads, plus a handful that are set up for top-roping. Grades run from the mid-5.6 range up to a few 5.11s, with the heart of the wall in the 5.8 to 5.10 range, so there is plenty for newer leaders and enough pump to stay interesting. The walk from the street is brief, which makes it a natural spot for a quick session after work. A modest set of quickdraws handles most lines.

ar_vestal.blurb: One of the sectors at Crystal Bluff, the urban crag above the Arkansas River at Big Rock Quarry in North Little Rock. Vestal holds 17 bolted sport lines of similar height, and the wall leans toward steep climbing. Grades begin near 5.7 and top out in the 5.12 range, with the middle of the spread, 5.9 to 5.11, getting most of the routes. Anything here needs to be led, since there is no easy way to reach the top. The approach is a short, steep trail from the base, and once at the top of it the wall is close by on one side.

yt_vinyl_village.blurb: A neighbourhood crag in Whitehorse, also known as The Acropolis, resting on the valley floor and therefore fairly shaded. Eighteen routes are on offer, with sport lines making up most of them and a few trad lines and a top-rope option in the mix. Grades start near 5.7 and reach into the low 5.12s, but the concentration is firmly at 5.10 and 5.11, which makes it a better fit for climbers with some mileage. Traffic is light, like many Yukon crags, and the town location keeps drive times short. Finding the street access for the first time is easier with a GPS track.

ar_ren_and_stimpy.blurb: A mostly bolted crag on the West Side of Horseshoe Canyon Ranch in north-central Arkansas, sixth wall along from the left. Seventeen lines are listed, fourteen of them sport and three trad. The grades lean hard: a few routes in the 5.9 range, a fair number of 5.10s and 5.11s, and a strong cluster in the 5.12 bracket. That makes it a good stop for climbers working the upper grades on the ranch's sandstone, and less of a place for a first lead. The West Side as a whole is a long wall that tends to stay shaded.

ar_goat_cave.blurb: A cave on the east side of Horseshoe Canyon Ranch in north-central Arkansas, mostly home to steep sport climbing with a few boulder problems tucked in. Sport lines start around 5.10 and are concentrated in the 5.11 and 5.12 range, while the boulder problems run from the mid-V grades into the double digits. The cave gets afternoon shade and is usually quiet, though expect to share the ground with the ranch's goats. The way in follows an ATV track that starts just past the gate on the entrance road, which makes it a shorter trip than the farther walls on this side.
